mbse_scope.value: Application of MBSE to space systems engineering at the system-of-interest level, organized around methods, languages, tools, and five proposed phases: requirements management, model development, simulation and analysis, configuration management, and collaboration and communication.

structured_model_scope.value: Requirements, behavioral, functional, logical, physical, executable, simulation, configuration, repository, and digital-thread representations used across space-system lifecycle work.

modeling_language_scope.value: General-purpose modeling languages (especially SysML, UML, and LML), domain-specific languages such as Modelica and AADL, programming or interface languages such as C/C++, Python, and APIs, and data-exchange syntax such as SQL, XMI, and XML.

tool_scope.value: Sixty-eight tools, frameworks, and libraries classified by reported function into modeling, design and simulation, model simulation, management, framework, and database or library categories.

artifact_scope.value: System models, requirements and architecture views, executable and simulation models, digital-thread and configuration artifacts, model repositories and libraries, reference models, and templates.

lifecycle_scope.value: Concept and technology development through preliminary and detailed design, assembly, integration and test, operations, and sustainment; the authors limit their proposed mapping to the system-of-interest layer.

model_generation_method_scope.value: The review extracts a named MBSE method for each included item and classifies methods into Pure, Enhanced, Extended, and Integrated archetypes. It mentions generation, transformation, reuse, and integration techniques, but does not systematically extract model origins, construction sources, ordered generation steps, decision logic, outputs, or checks.

generic_or_reference_model_construction_.value: CubeSat reference models, standardized templates, model libraries, reference architectures, and reusable patterns are identified, but their source selection, synthesis, abstraction, traceability, and genericity checks are not reviewed systematically.

engineering_workflow_scope.value: A five-phase MBSE workflow abstraction links requirements management, model development, simulation and analysis, configuration management, and collaboration and communication to lifecycle stages and classes of enablers.

procedure_reporting_scope.value: The report explains the proposed phases and selected examples at a high level, while its study-level synthesis table records method, language, tool, mission, and phase flags rather than ordered construction, workflow, or tailoring procedures and supporting materials.

generic_model_procedural_evidence_scope.value: Generic, reference, and template artifacts are named and mapped to enablers, but the review does not link them systematically to actionable construction or tailoring procedures, worked tailoring examples, or post-tailoring assurance.

artifact_reuse_and_tailoring_scope.value: The review covers model reuse, design-reuse libraries, patterns, templates, reference models, and the need to tailor frameworks to mission scale. It does not consistently extract applicability bounds, reusable cores, variation points, tailoring rules or steps, independent applications, or post-tailoring checks.

method_reuse_and_adaptation_scope.value: Methods are grouped by maturity and application scope and discussed as context-dependent or tailored, but stable method cores, variation points, adaptation steps, repeated applications, and assurance are not bounded systematically.

workflow_reuse_and_adaptation_scope.value: The five phases are presented as a modular adoption guide and reusable toolchains are discussed, but reusable workflow definitions, stable handoffs, variation points, executed adaptations, and assurance are not extracted at study level.

outcome_scope.value: Reported functional contributions of methods, languages, and tools to systems-engineering tasks, including traceability, architecture understanding, simulation, optimization, reliability and mission assurance, interoperability, configuration control, collaboration, lifecycle continuity, and adoption effectiveness.

burden_scope.value: Training, tool selection and licensing, customization and integration effort, resource and time intensity, fragmented toolchains and languages, semantic loss, organizational maturity, uncertain return on investment, and disproportionate burden for lightweight missions.

verification_and_validation_scope.value: Broad space-system model-based V&V, simulation, reliability and safety analyses, executable checks, virtual testbeds, architecture validation, and model-to-integration continuity, chiefly within the simulation-and-analysis and configuration-management phases.

crd3_eligibility_criteria_and_applicatio.value: Eligible reports, peer-reviewed articles, and conference papers had to contain MBSE applied to a space mission of any type or size. citations.quote: Received: 1 December 2023 Revised: 8 December 2025 Accepted: 19 February 2026

This comprehensive review analyzes 126 studies published between 2011 and 2023 to examine current MBSE practices and their enablers (method, tool, and language) to identify the best strategies of application.

This paper presents a literature review on MBSE applications for space SE, aiming to synthesize best practices and identify strategic patterns that support standardized adoption across diverse mission contexts.

The comprehensive literature review (CLR) was conducted using the PRISMA guidelines as reference for a review procedure [34]. This investigation focuses exclusively on the application of MBSE within domain of space system engineering. It includes a wide range of studies covering various mission types from CubeSats to complex crewed missions.

- RQ1: How have MBSE methodologies and their capabilities evolved? This question investigates the range of MBSE methods applied in space engineering and examines implementation patterns across the literature.

- RQ2: What MBSE modeling languages and syntax are employed and what roles do they play across the SE lifecycle? This question identifies the languages and syntax used in MBSE application and examines their roles in supporting specific SE tasks.

- RQ3: What tools are used to support MBSE implementation? This RQ retrieves MBSE tools referenced in the literature, analyzing their frequency utilization, and mapping their capabilities.

- RQ4: What are the relationship between the MBSE phases and enablers? This question investigates how combinations of MBSE enablers contribute to achieving targeted SE objective and clarifies the realization of MBSE phases across the system lifecycle.

- RQ5: What challenges are identified in the literature and how does the proposed method address them to improve MBSE application in space systems? This question explores the technical and methodological challenges observed in current practices and assesses how the proposed method offers opportunities for improved MBSE adoption and future research directions.

The databases of selected literature are Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science (WoS). The following keywords are used for these databases: "model-based systems engineering," "MBSE," and "space." In the WoS database, the keywords "MBSE" and "space" were used, yielding a total of 170 publications. As of December 31, 2022, this search extracted 170 articles. The extracted publications include the years 2011-2022. A Scopus search in February 2023 resulted in 191 articles extracted from conferences, proceedings, and journal articles.

Following the pre-eligibility phase, 266 articles and reports were screened after eliminating duplicate studies. The application of inclusion and exclusion criteria was carried out based on title, publication year, keywords, and search exclusions. The rest of selection criteria required a detailed review of the study content.

citations.quote: 1. Included study types from all sources are reports, peer-reviewed journals, and conference papers

2. The research must contain space mission applications using MBSE.

3. Inclusive of all types and sizes of space missions (subsystems and space segment development, and existing missions).

After the selection process according to the inclusion criteria is complete, the exclusion criteria are applied as follows:

1. All studies published before 2011 are omitted; this was applied during the database search.

2. Antenna deployment, embedded system, and software development applications through MBSE are excluded, despite their development for space, as this study focuses on the core subsystems of the space segment.

3. Aeronautics, defense, and naval application studies are not considered in space engineering; therefore, 24 studies were excluded based on nonspace application criteria.

4. The study of MBSE in space science discussion on mission exploration: 12 studies are removed under this criteria

5. The studies presenting comparison and experience report, overviews of programs, or evaluation studies all are also eliminated: 13 studies are excluded.

6. The remaining 20 studies full content were inaccessible from source database.

The review process was conducted step by step using multiple publication source. The initial search carried out in the WoS database yielded 170 articles, followed by a search in Scopus database on March 20, 2023, which identified 192 additional articles. From April to December 2023, the comprehensive review analysis and manuscript preparation were complete. After applying the selection criteria, 126 articles and reports were selected for detailed review.

Initially, each study was mapped to one or more of the five MBSE phases to determine primary focus of the application, as summarized in Table 1. Then, the research questions RQ1, RQ2, and RQ3 were addressed by extracting and performing a quantitative analysis of the modeling languages, methods, and tools used in each study. For RQ4, a qualitative analysis was conducted to examine relationship MBSE phases and enablers across the overall system lifecycle, as described Section 2.1. RQ5 explored challenges and opportunities through qualitative synthesis and cross analysis derived from the prior RQs. In addition, supplementary statistical data such as publication year, country, affiliation, journal type, and publisher were also analyzed. Inter-rater reliability assessment was conducted to validate the consistency and reliability of article classification. The synthesis was carried out using Excel and full synthesis tables are provided in Appendices B-E.

A bottom-up, inductive approach was used for categorizing methods, justified by the absence of a uniform classification and the need to group novel techniques based on bibliometric and contextual similarity. In next step, the coding of MBSE languages was systematically mapped from the encapsulated tools and their interactions, as delineated in the literature.

We observed that some studies did not explicitly specify the MBSE tools and languages during the data extraction process. In many cases, especially in technical solution-oriented studies, the specific language used was omitted or not clearly distinguished. However, the omission rate for tools is minimal (less than 1%) which allowed languages to be inferred directly from the tools used. Overall, the classification includes 126 distinct methods, seven languages, and 68 tools.

The validity of the study is evaluated by three external reviewers, who possess expertise in MBSE, the space industry, and academia, to avoid default agreement between the authors. The inter-rater reliability determines the agreement between the experts' and the author's classification in each section.

The assessment of reliability was used as feedback to identify and resolve classification ambiguity and to strengthen the credibility of the results. Reflecting on the lower level of agreement in the MBSE methodologies and tools, we have refined the classification scheme to eliminate ambiguity and adjust the process accordingly.

Studies focused on spacecraft subsystem development account for 34% followed by CubeSat missions at 23% and SmallSat missions at 21%. Larger missions are also represented, including crewed missions (11%), large missions (8%), and deep space exploration (3%), such as the Europa and James Webb Telescopes.

A total of 126 distinct MBSE methods were extracted from the reviewed articles and subsequently classified by their methodological maturity, diversity of applications, and degree customization to meet growing demand in the space industry.

Another emerging application is an AI-enabled security service, such as a quantum key distribution developed for encryption purposes to secure linked nanosatellites [123]. The coordination of agile processes and MBSE tools facilitates the development of encryption process standards by leveraging the behaviors of the system and subsystem [123].
The challenge of achieving interoperability between modeling languages and various system programming and data languages is clearly shown in Figure 13.

The CubeSat reference model (CSRM) was studied, while the CubeSat mission undergoes a development stages in consecutive studies using several tools [92,140-142]. It serves as an exemplary instance of MBSE application, necessitating a diverse array of tools for modeling, design, simulation, management, and a collaborative framework toolchain and libraries throughout the various stages of the development lifecycle.

Frameworks represent an organized integration of several tools with interfacing techniques, serving the shared purpose of enabling emphasizing high-intensity data interoperability between modeling, simulation, and management tools. This location of tools within the same digital environment ensures data compatibility and minimizes data transfer errors during the MBSE process.

In general, MBSE implementation through an enterprise approach considers the entire ecosystem to ensure comprehensive adoption. This strategy supports the alignment of MBSE phases with the project lifecycle, considering both operational and project-level views. The relationship discussed above between the phases and modeling enablers highlights the usability of MBSE artifacts and SE activities, providing significant value in determining whether objectives are met and results are actionable.

Extended and Integrated MBSE approaches have shown flexible and broader lifecycle applicability but resource-intensive and time-consuming. In contrast, Enhanced MBSE yields effective results for discipline-focused experts, with expense of limited applicability and introduces heterogeneity when attempting to scale for lifecycle coverage.

This is particularly salient for the implementation of CubeSat and university-led missions, which entail a disproportionate burden of cost and resources, rendering legacy MBSE implementation impractical. The exploration of lightweight and scalable MBSE strategies that do not compromise potential benefits remains largely unexamined.

This study had a significant scope of coverage; however, it encountered several notable limitations. Access-restricted publications and the potential exclusion of relevant articles from databases outside primary sources and variant date search posed completeness of dataset.

During synthesis, the marked (X) phases refer to a topic discussed in an individual study, but may not reflect the full extent of MBSE implementation, as some missions may have engaged in earlier or later phases not captured in paper. Additionally, ambiguity in the reported use of MBSE enablers, where methods, language, and tools were used interchangeably and loosely referred to as "MBSE," posed classification challenges. The classification of MBSE approaches was challenging due to the insufficient evidence regarding the depth or breadth of application within the papers studies. The tool capabilities described in this review are based solely on the tasks reported in the studies; some tools may offer broader or more functionalities than those stated. While the phases used in this review overlap with the system lifecycle and possess an interconnected relationship, this relationship map is incomplete due to the scope of this review being limited to the SoI layer.

Resource mismatched MBSE frameworks for lightweight or small scale missionsThis paper introduces a classification of MBSE approach (Pure, Enhanced, Extended, and Integrated) promoting tailored adoption for mission scale and maturity with example of open source tools.Develop modular scalable MBSE frameworks and adoption playbooks for resource constrained missions (e.g., CubeSats), focusing on cost-effectiveness, rapid prototyping, and mission assurance trade-offs.

Finally, the underlying gap identified is that only a few studies explicitly demonstrate how MBSE supports the mission objectives. This lack of a targeted objective and the limited interpretation of the MBSE application may be a root cause for dispersed efforts and a lack of measurable outcomes (RQ5).
